The biggest truth right here. Even now I have kales, fava beans, and lettuces that will awaken when spring comes. I have compost slowly rotting that will become humus. And I have a gift card I will use to start an awesome indoor nursery.
I need to order my new plants for the year soon. Got a few that are wintering, but there will be some empty patches that need filling too.

Trying to decide when to start all of my seeds this year. Last year I started them late feb/early march on the recommendation on the seed packets but the minimal sunlight we get here in the spring made them about a month behind. Then again, this year I have an LED light to help the seedlings, BUT it's currently occupied with my indoor tomato plant and may be until summer.

I'll tell you from my experience, I don't like to start my seeds too early. I started most of mine in march last year and they did fine.

Big plants don't always mean well adapted plants. 6 months in artificial light, soil, and heat means they will be expecting the same conditions. If they're not hardened off well enough, they get sunburned, shocked by cold soil and air temps, and often try to flower too soon as a survival mechanism.

Last year I put my tomatoes in after the last frost in April. They barely grew for a month or so as they were adapting to outdoor conditions. And yet, they bare fruit at the same time, tasted fine, and lasted all year.

Starting seeds indoors is meant to give a small jump start in my opinion, not half a year.

We're coming out of a really cold snap so it's time to fill the water shed and get more firewood into the house. A neighbor had his water freeze underground, so we spent a couple of days letting them shower and laundry at our house while we got it sorted. Having the ability to work comfortably at the worst weather is important. It was -38C plus the wind and I was able to lay on the ground for an hour at a time before warming up. Having several sources of heat and the skills to repair them has been valuable this winter!

Also found out that sewing machine oil isn't light enough to allow a gun to operate at these temperatures, it works find down to -30, but the extra 8 degrees was the straw. I had to strip the bolt, clean out all the oil, and run it dry. I'm going to try arctic moly grease next. Fwiw, the fancy north american and german guns are under gassed at these temps and cracked plastic, we found the russian crap runs like butter. The SVT-40 was especially good (once we set the gas up a couple of holes).
